title: How do you feel about AI agents to replace scripted NPCs?
author: Marceloo25
selftext:
I've been working on a concept for a game where each NPC in a village is replaced by an AI agent. It's based on a Standford study "Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior".

One thing I try to fix in the paper is cost. So I always make sure that this also works with fully self hosted models. Locally I can run a Qwen 3.5 with 9B parameters and Piper for voice and I don't see any performance loss. Only quality loss. But I'm also running it on a 3090.

Video: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzyQBu-9o9Q](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzyQBu-9o9Q)

Note: My next goal for this project is to explore de concept of an AI GM.

comments.author: ManagerOfClankers
comments.body: Prohibitive cost wise either utilizes cloud or requires the user to have a fat GPU

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
Actually, there've been a number of studies done to make tiny (2-5B parameter) models actually beat out SotA models in niche areas. The more specific your use case, the better the results. I expect that you could have an AI making very good decisions and delivering excellent interactions within constrained bounds (so not an AI that just does anything like an open story, but by giving them specific tools to interact with that do things like initiate an engagement, make decisions based on their inventory or pricing, trade, etc ) on one of these models that even a shitty laptop can run at high speeds. Yeah it won't be a phone game, but assuming your graphical demands are not already high (like I wouldn't throw this into Cyberpunk or something) it should be a free addition. The biggest hurdle is putting together a well crafted dataset with enough parameters to make it stick and finetuning a powerful, small qwen or gemma. I think to develop that dataset you'd probably have to use a SotA model and an iterative curation process to actually build out those 10k+ samples. But it's definitely within the realm of possibility. And you could expand upon that dataset for future iterations of the model by setting up some kind of performative review process in game wherwer ea player could rate an interaction and consistently highly rated ones get shuffled into a training set for review (and likewise poorly rated ones could lead to some investigation into why something happened or what it might have to be trained to handle.

Definitely not a plug and play system th ough. We're talking a large amount of work just for preparing the training data, not to mention subsequent testing, or even setting up the constraints  and data format you'd need the AI to respond to to begin with. But really that's the only way to get the 99+% consistency in output that you'd need to make it reasonable. I think anything less than that and I'd prefer a completely deterministic system over AI breaking a quest because the model hallucinated.

replies.author: ManagerOfClankers
replies.body: Could, can, lots of if ands and buts lol.  You're not getting there with any sort of ease... especially image breakdown and puzzle solving. You need a bigger model for that... unless they are predetermined puzzles in which, you can just use code not an LLM or LMM

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
Image breakdown and puzzle solving? Well sure, I guess if we're talking very specific niche uses.

I agree that most of it can be handled by deterministic systems with weighted oracles for decisions. In fact that's what I used in my own game. I, however, used a small LLM specifically trained for dialogue and interactions so that even if it was something like offering a quest (the deterministic part) it would be worded differently depending on the personality markers of the NPC and on what the player actually said in the conversation. I could not think of any way to deterministically set up such an emergent system without the assistance of an LLM. And there are no concerns with things like 'image breakdown' or 'puzzle solving' as that's not remotely relevant to what that model is being used for.

replies.author: TriggerHydrant
replies.body: So with the right model one could build a custom ‘NPC DIALOG’ system that could run locally?

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body: Yes. You finetune the model to handle a jsonb that will carry the 'intent' of the dialogue, information on the speaker, setting, or whatever else you need delivered, and then receives back a response from the AI that composes a natural language delivery as if it was that character responding in whichever way you instructed it to (generally better to have a deterministic game action rather than let the AI decide, as that starts to spread the model's responsibility and that can cause issues with smaller models). So if the intent is to have the NPC ask the player to help them deal with some goblins that have been ravaging the town's food supply, you could have an oracle in the back end have marked that npc as affected in some way (personal loss, economic loss, whatever) from the goblins, pass that along as part of the jsonb, the model returns with the merchant/innkeeper/farmer talking about his dead chickens and needing help clearing the goblins out. If you want to get fancy you could have an additional deliverable like a customized quest log entry that is simultaneously written for the designated quest. In the back-end, the requirements for fulfilling it are handled deterministically (goblin encounter beaten at X location or whatever) but all the text the user sees is customized to make it feel like a unique experience instead of, "Kill ten goblins. Reward: 10 xp"

comments.author: 0bscuris
comments.body:
My experience with this is that you end up spending alot of resource to get back to somewhere you could more easily get by just writing the dialogue.

I tried letting llm do the whole thing just prompting with character description and situation, incosistent results, lag on bigger models, output still fairly generic. 

I tried giving the llm generic text, then telling it ur this character modify this text to be in their voice. It either modified too much and lost the message or under modified it. 

I tried letting the llm choose between existing dialogue based on the inferred tone of player input. I can do this better and faster with dialogue tree and tags. 

I tried using a decision tree of llm size, so that basic conversation was handled by dumber models and more important characters by smarter ones, just added a bunch of over processing and lag, fairly generic results. 

I do agree that ai gm-ing is coming. But i think we arn’t there yet on hardware and software. I suspect the first version will be something like roll 20 or dnd beyond leasing an ai, training it on dnd campaigns and then offering it as a “dm aid” and it will use cloud ai.

comments.author: Old_Swan8945

Not saying it’s technically impossible but more you’d have to figure out how to get an LLM character to work at all, and even today the best LLM characters we have are AI girlfriend/boyfriend type things

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body:
It's good in theory but it's similar to why NPCs combat AI is often dumbed down - because it's just not fun. If the NPCs are GenAI LLMs then the player is going to spend a bit of time trying to jailbreak the system and have them say world-inappropriate things for laughs, or they'll just get the gist in the first 5-10 minutes and just want to get to the point.   
  
It doesn't enhance the game for as much as it costs (both in monetary terms if you're paying for LLM API costs, or the cost of the delays waiting for the LLM to generate dialog if it's generated locally. LLMs aren't very interesting to talk to in-depth and generative AI storytelling isn't at the same place as just pre-writing stories and having the player play them.
